question: According to the Brewers of Europe report on ‘European Beer Trends 2026’, beer consumption in the EU in 2025 was 3.2 % lower than in the previous year and 9.2 % lower than in 2019, with production decreasing by 8.6 % over the same period. At the same time, the sector provides around 2 million jobs and EUR 52 billion in added value and is considered an important part of the European agricultural, cultural and tourism sectors. 1.
What is the Commission’s assessment of the economic and cultural importance of the brewing sector for the European agri-food sector and rural areas?
What measures does the Commission plan to take to support small and medium-sized breweries in the face of falling consumption and rising costs?
What scope does the Commission see for supporting the sector’s innovative capacity and competitiveness through targeted programmes?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (4.9.2026) 1. According to Eurostat, beer ranks as the EU’s third highest-value manufactured food and beverage product by production value1. The brewing sector is connected to the European agrifood sector through its demand for agricultural raw materials, notably barley, wheat and hops.
This demand supports agricultural production, malting, and other upstream and downstream activities, including in rural areas where many of these crops are grown and processed. 2.

Small and medium-sized breweries can benefit from EU initiatives supporting small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), such as the Enterprise Europe Network, which can, among other things, help drive innovation through digital and sustainable solutions and facilitate access to EU funding2.

The Network has a dedicated Agri-Food Sector Group, composed of experienced advisors supporting SMEs in the food and beverage sector. 3. The innovative capacity of the sector can be supported through initiatives in areas such as the bioeconomy, including the Circular Bio-based Europe Joint Undertaking (CBE JU). A relevant project supported under the CBE JU is POLYMEER, which aims to valorise brewers’ spent grain3.

In addition, the sector’s competitiveness can be strengthened through improved access to international markets. For example, the EU–India Free Trade Agreement will, once in force, reduce tariffs on beer from 110% to 50%4.
